t: How To Handle A Bully Principal
q: They come in every size and shape, stripe and strata of education. And although their methods of torment may differ, the way to deal with them is the same: Don’t give them an opportunity.
Nothing gets under a principal’s skin more than having to deal with behavior issues. They have enough to worry about.
Be a pillar of competency and hang on tight to your self-worth. It’s the grovelers and sycophants who take the brunt of a wrathful boss.
Again, when your principal can count on you, when you don’t add stress to their already stressful life, they become deeply grateful you’re a member of the staff.
When you act nervously and walk on eggshells and worry over this and that you make the principal suspicious that perhaps you don’t have your act together.
I did my job well so nothing she could have said would have mattered.
And even if it is, most of the time it’s avoidable. If currently find yourself in the crosshairs, then follow the guidelines above. Slowly but surely, in a few weeks, they’ll forget about you.

t: A Perfect Definition of the Best Place in the World
q: Shoe (so nicknamed because he looks like legendary jockey Willie Shoemaker) proves that leadership can be exemplified in the processes and diligence of individuals who simply care.
He digs, spending time on the internet searching towns and backgrounds, photos and posts, looking for a connection, a way to spark a conversation that will make people feel known and welcome.
When golfers arrive, many far from home, they learn that someone special has taken the time to know who they are.
Shoe knows secrets. He knows the best place in the world is the place that knows you best.
People like to be known and the leaders and people who take the time to know them are worthy of great admiration.
He knows people like to be remembered more than they like just about anything else.

t: What Schools Should Do With the Billions Coming Their Way
q: That sounds straightforward, but the term could just mean there’s one study showing positive effects. Meanwhile, there could be—and often are—more studies that go the other way.

That approach mirrors the standard elementary curriculum, and it won’t work any better with tutoring than it has in the classroom. Reading comprehension depends far more on academic knowledge and vocabulary than on abstract “skill”—which is probably why studies show that with reading tutoring, there’s “a pattern of declining returns” at higher grade levels.

Because of the dominance of reading and math at lower grade levels, kids often arrive at high school without the background knowledge they need to succeed. That’s particularly true if they’ve had limited opportunities to acquire academic knowledge outside school.
It’s best to use the same curriculum across as many grades as possible. Building knowledge is a gradual, cumulative process.

But withholding academic knowledge from children and then holding them accountable for knowing it, as we currently do, is the essence of unfairness. And large majorities of students lack basic knowledge of history and civics, something that jeopardizes not only their own futures but the future of our democracy.

But rather than trying to reinvent the wheel, districts should adopt an existing curriculum and add or substitute materials that cover what they feel is missing. Creating curriculum from scratch is hard, and most educators haven’t been trained to do it.

t: Scan Others for Clues About You
q: Really knowing yourself requires genuine insight and often takes years to do.
Knowing the many facets of yourself is a critical pursuit. And self contemplation only goes so far.
The truth is, people don’t like to tell us what they really think.
The best leaders know the secret step in this process — observation.
By watching how others respond to what we say and do, we cut through the red tape of getting candid feedback.
People may hide their perceptions, but they are lousy at masking their reactions.

t: The Town Where Almost All the Children Are Gifted
q: So administrators decided that any student who responded to instruction in regular classrooms and took standardized tests—that is, who didn’t need serious remedial services—would qualify as “gifted.” And voila: the vast majority of Charlottesville students are now “gifted,” with representation of Black and Hispanic students roughly equivalent to their proportions in the school population: 33% are Black, 14% Hispanic, and 42% white.

So it may come as unsettling news to those on both sides that gifted programs, on average, aren’t correlated with increases in test scores. A recent study drawing on data from about 18,000 elementary students across the U.S. found that receiving gifted services for a year or more was associated with no statistically significant gains in math and only a slight bump in reading—and Black and most low-income students didn’t even experience that slight bump. Nor was there any benefit in terms of engagement or motivation.
A large 2019 survey of elementary schools found that most gifted programs focus on projects, games, and activities intended to develop critical thinking and creativity.
But gifted programs will never work as a way to advance equity because our system routinely squanders the potential of huge numbers of children.
The more you know about the topic you’re reading about, the better your comprehension. And the more general academic knowledge you have, the more likely you are to understand whatever you read.

This standard approach may explain why many gifted programs apparently have little effect. If they just provide more “skills” practice but don’t build kids’ substantive knowledge, they’re likely to be just as ineffective as such practice in regular classrooms.

Teachers who have switched to curricula that dive deeply into substantive topics have told me that all their students have blossomed—but especially kids who previously would have been relegated to “low” reading groups. It’s the English-language learners or the children identified as needing special education, they’ve said, who often make the most insightful contributions to class discussion, bringing up concepts and vocabulary introduced months before.

t: How To Handle A Bully Colleague
q: But in the long run you’ll be so glad you took it. Not only for your own peace of mind and self-worth, but because it weakens the bully and their power over you.
Bullies are cowards, and they can’t stand eye contact. By just looking them in the eye—and holding it—whenever they make a snide remark, you make them uncomfortable.
To resist, I’ve found that just saying “No, I’m not going to do that”—and then holding your ground with direct eye contact—is the most powerful response.
Don’t go back on your word. Don’t argue your point. Just stick to your guns, unmovable, like an iron stake hammered into frozen ground.
But if you’re consistent and don’t give in, they’ll back down. They’ll stop speaking to you or even looking in your direction.
Calmly say, “I don’t want to hear advice from you again” or “never again tell me what to do.

t: 3 Simple Ways to Practice Classroom Management on Your Kids This Summer https://davestuartjr.com/3-simple-ways-to-practice-classroom-management-on-your-kids-this-summer
q: I was a teacher for ten years. I’ve been a parent for four. When I make mistakes in parenting and wind up with a Whopper Freak Out, it’s almost always because I’m neglecting a basic tenet of good classroom management.

It’s the difference between “Go brush your teeth,” and “When I say ‘Go,' walk to the bathroom, pick up your blue toothbrush, take out the toothpaste, unscrew the cap, squeeze a tiny bit on the bristles, and brush back and forth. Ready? Go!
In our classrooms, we make the weather. We have to maintain a demeanor that is pleasant and likable no matter what baggage students bring through our doors or what emotions they let loose.
But the visible annoyance NEVER makes things better and almost always makes things worse. So we must practice a different response.
First, I make a clear rule: Stay in your own bed. If he breaks this rule and gets out of bed once, he gets a warning.
So this summer, practice giving a small consequence consistently. Pick an area of your day in which your kids are breaking a rule and driving you crazy. Name the clear rule and the consequence.
And you will, because you practiced on your own kids — or on nieces, nephews, and neighbors — all summer long.

t: Efficiency Matters and Perfection is a Mirage: Updates to the Article of the Week for 2021-2022
q: Since all my students had computers and some of them were remote or quarantining at any given time, I found the process of converting each week's article into a PDF or Google Doc needlessly cumbersome.
Because I'm eager for my students to learn as much as they can — and because 1:1 decreased the friction of sharing articles with my students — I started using articles more than 1x/week.

When I found an interesting article that related to any of our burning questions of the year or current topics of interest in our curriculum, I could easily incorporate it into my lessons — no need to copy/paste/format/print/etc.

I still dislike the added distraction that a computer's web browser presents — for children and for adults. Reading articles on a news website inevitably means exposure to advertisements and temptations to Ctl+T your way into a (likely defocusing) new tab/game/experience.

So, like normal, ain't no silver bullets and no perfect scenarios. However, for me the life-enhancing, democratizing and emancipating power of a knowledge-rich curricula outweighs the drawbacks of added sources of distraction and periodically annoying paywalls.
As always, remember that we're each responsible for the articles we share with our students. Know your setting, know your community, know your administrators.
Know what you're after: student long-term flourishing via optimized mastery outcomes without sacrificing your life on the altar of professional success. Pursue this doggedly.

t: Substitute Teaching in the Atlanta Area School for the Deaf
q: I had also assumed that ASL was communicated through hands alone—that the static pictures of signs you may have seen are the entire meaning of the word one communicates in ASL. Lara clarified, however, that ASL is communicated through hands moving multidimensionally through space, at different speeds, attached to a person with a face making expressions, the sum of which can endow communication in ASL more nuance and meaning than the same words in spoken English.

Lara told me that deaf kids often suffer from language deprivation since many deaf children are not exposed to an accessible language early in life. While hearing babies are constantly absorbing and learning language just by existing in a world full of spoken words, deaf babies and children often don’t receive the same resources, informally or even formally.

Mathematics is a discipline that delights in its nuances and distinctions. (It isn’t just a triangle, it’s an obtuse triangle. It isn’t just a number, it’s a rational number.) And my students and I were going to have very different languages for communicating nuance and distinction.

One consequence of that deprivation is that my deaf students could more accurately express their thinking about prisms in ASL, a language I don’t understand, than they could in written English, a language I do understand. So the students would express their ideas in ASL to their interpreter who would express them verbally to me—a game of telephone with everyone using different languages and having different kinds of knowledge about the subject they're trying to discuss.

I said throughout the lesson, as much to remind myself as to communicate it to students, "Other mathematicians have defined prisms differently from you folks, but your mind and your eyes are working together to produce some really interesting thinking.

We're always teaching students whose ideas about mathematics—the patterns they're noticing, their estimations about quantities and shapes, etc.—outstrip their ability to express them. It's perhaps more obvious when students haven’t received adequate instruction in written English or when their primary language is different from ours. But I'm grateful for the reminder that there is always more going on in a student's mind than meets our eyes or ears.
x: ASL is a distinct language with multidimensional, visual features, and some math ideas may be explained more clearly in it than in English.
Language deprivation means written English can understate what deaf students actually think about a concept.
What students know, what they can express, and what the teacher grasps of that expression are different sets that only partly overlap.

t: Should You Allow Your Students To Talk During Independent Work?
q: Independent practice is the most critical factor in developing academic skill and competency.
But talking, even whispering? Like a surprised knock on your front door, it cuts straight through to the prefrontal cortex, breaking concentration in an instant.
It takes several minutes of quiet focus to get into a state of flow , whereby time slips by unnoticed, performance soars, and the very act of doing the work becomes an enjoyable experience.

Independence is a muscle students develop through daily practice. It results in an ability – a superpower in this day and age of shortening attention spans – they can enjoy and carry with them into the future.
One thing is for sure, if you do allow talking, then the ability to attend will weaken for all students. You’ll create a dependent, immature class that can’t sit still for more than ten minutes.
You take care of all of this beforehand by preparing your students to succeed all on their own—yes, every student—and without help from you, their classmates, or anyone else.

Even whispered talking breaks concentration instantly because the brain reflexively tries to decipher what's being said.
Repeated interruptions prevent students from reaching a productive state of flow, turning independent work into a dreaded slog.

q: Usually, this has been in the form of a self-evaluation sheet guiding me to consider how and when I can use the CPD in my practice. I have to admit that when filling these forms, either I have written down something that I had already been doing and simply matched it to the CPD I was reflecting on, or I have written down something I genuinely wanted to try out but then didn’t for various reasons.

One of these reasons is that it is really hard to change habits. But keeping the same habits can make it harder for us to be effective teachers and can stifle our improvement, according to this eye-opening research by Hobbiss et al. So when it comes to CPD, it is important I remove any barriers so that I can committ to applying CPD to my practice. One way I can achieve this is by making small, manageable changes to my practice that are in line with CPD I undertake but that don’t radically change the way I teach.

Besides CPD, one of the most important ways to improve our practice is by reflecting on the lessons we teach. I find it so helpful when I teach the same topic to different classes in a year group. By the third time I have explained enzyme action in a week, the wording and the way I introduce examples and explanations are close to perfect (I am forever reflecting on how to improve further, which is why I don’t consider it perfect!).

But what if, following reflection of a lesson, I come to the wrong conclusion or, more realistically, a conclusion that is not exactly right? For example, when teaching a class, I may find that promising 5 minutes of ‘free time’ at the end of a lesson makes students work well. I reflect on this lesson and come to the conslusion that with this class, giving them free time is an excellent motivator, and I continue using this practice.
Reflecting is vital to improving our practice but there can be a fine line between reflecting and overthinking. I have certainly been guilty of the latter.

This is definitely applicable to teaching too! The more I read and the more conversations I have, the more I can effectively reflect with purpose. I may not get everything right each time, but thinking about why that is and relating it to past experience, other peoples’ experiences, and what the research says, can only serve to help.
